newsitem.title: USA: News reports show changes in Ohio school district.
newsitem.headline: News reports show changes in Ohio school district.

text.p: The Plain Dealer series on the borrowing practices of the financially strapped Cleveland schools from 1992 to 1995 actually reveals the "dramatic changes" in the district since the state takeover of the system, a schools spokesman said Tuesday.
While it remains on the Ohio auditor's fiscal emergency list, the district has improved its financial outlook under the state's guidance, spokesman Rick Ellis said.
As it has several times over the past 20 years, the district must again look to short-term borrowing to meet operating expenses in the next month, Ellis noted.
The district plans to borrow $90 million in the next few weeks to meet its payroll obligations for the rest of the school fiscal year, which ends on June 30, Ellis noted.
Current state rules permit the district to borrow for only a two-year period, Ellis said. The district plans to seek legislative changes that would allow it to borrow over a 10-year period, he said.
Until voters approved a levy last November, the schools had planned for borrowing up to $150 million, Ellis said.

Based on an initial reading of the series, and without formal discussion, the articles allege poor management, but it appears no state laws were broken, said Tom Prendergast, spokesman for Ohio Auditor Jim Petro.
If asked, the state auditor's special audit committee would make a preliminary review of the allegations, Prendergast said.

If a review determines "a good possibility" that public money was illegally spent or unaccounted for, then a special audit could begin, Prendergast said. If not, the allegations could be dealt with in the annual audit, he said.

McDonald & Company Securities Inc. has said in a terse statement that it disagreed with The Plain Dealer series and was "disappointed by the paper's distorted portrayal of our firm's work in public finance."
McDonald cooperated with the newspaper investigation and was "sorry" its input was given little weight, the statement continued.
McDonald also said that the newspaper "opted to abandon any pretense of objectivity in its coverage of this story."
